# Book 1, Chapter 1: The Discovery

## Part One: 789 — The Scored Ground

The limestone was scored.

Luca knelt in the high Pollino meadow, running his fingers across the pale stone where, three months ago, only grass had grown. The marks were fresh—not weathered smooth by a season, not rounded by rain. Sharp. Deliberate. As if something massive had dug in and pushed.

He was fourteen years old and had never seen anything like it.

The shepherd paths that crossed these heights were older than memory. Luca had walked them since he could stand, following his father's flocks through the seasonal pasture rotations, learning to read the mountain the way other boys learned to read the faces of their kin. He knew where the storm runoff cut channels. He knew which rocks shifted in spring melt. He knew the difference between a goat's hoof-scuff and the deep scoring that came when an animal fought for purchase on loose shale.

This was not any of those things.

He looked up from the marked stone. The ancient pine stood thirty paces higher on the slope, massive and solitary, its crown rising above the surrounding scrub like a sentinel. Heldreich's pine—his mother called them that, using the formal name her own mother had taught her, the kind of name mountain people held onto when the lowland towns forgot what things really were. This particular tree had been here longer than the village where Luca's family kept their secondary winter shelter. Longer than anyone could say. The trunk was thick as the width of three men shoulder to shoulder, the bark dark and furrowed, the crown dense with the short needles that distinguished the species from its smaller cousins.

Luca had seen this tree perhaps fifty times in his life, maybe more. It was a landmark. A place to shelter from sudden rain. A reference point when the mist came down and direction became uncertain.

He had never paid it particular attention.

The scoring, though. The scoring was new.

He stood and moved upslope toward the tree, his boots finding purchase on stones he'd crossed a thousand times. The June afternoon was warm, the kind of afternoon that made the shadows seem deeper and the air itself more substantial. A storm had passed through four days ago—summer lightning, the kind that came late in the day and spent itself quickly. Luca remembered it clearly because it had scattered one of his father's herds across two ridges and cost him half a night of recovery work, moving the animals back together, checking for injuries in the dim light before moonrise.

He'd attributed the scattered herd to the noise and light of the storm itself.

Now, examining the ground around the pine's base, he reconsidered.

The soil was disturbed. Not recently—Luca could read soil the way other people read text. There was a difference between a disturbance hours old and one from days past. This looked to be roughly four days old, the edges of the disturbed earth beginning to oxidize, the loose material starting to settle. Roots were exposed where they shouldn't be, where Luca was certain they hadn't been exposed before. The massive taproot system that anchored the tree had shifted.

Not much. Perhaps two feet from where he remembered it. Perhaps more. He had never measured precisely. He had only passed the tree, known it was there, thought nothing of it.

His heart was moving faster than the exertion justified.

Luca circled the tree's base slowly, cataloging details with the same methodical attention he used when searching for lost animals. The northeast quadrant showed the most disturbance. The south side, facing the lower slope, had fresh resin bleeding from a long gouge in the bark, maybe eight feet up from ground level—resin that looked pale and still sticky where the bark had been stripped. He'd never seen the tree bleeding resin like that before.

The western roots had pulled tight, he thought. Compressed. The eastern roots seemed looser, as if they'd been the anchor point for leverage.

It was as if the tree had moved. Shifted its entire weight, used the leverage of its root system to pull itself incrementally across the stone.

Which was impossible.

Trees did not move.

Luca sat down on the disturbed soil and stared at the tree, his mind working through the problem like a dog worrying at a piece of leather. Lightning could damage bark. Storms could shift soil and wash away earth. High winds could lean a standing tree, make it seem to occupy a different position in space.

But the scoring on the limestone. That was not wind damage. That was not water erosion. That was something pressing down and moving across stone, leaving marks as if an enormous hand had dragged fingernails across the surface.

He sat for a long time in the afternoon heat, watching the tree. The tree, naturally, did not move. It was rooted in place, its branches moving slightly in the light wind, its needles catching the slanted sunshine. To any observer, it was exactly what it had always been: a massive, ancient tree, standing where trees stood.

Luca got to his feet and began the walk back down the slope toward the village. He moved slowly, his mind still on the scored stone and the displaced roots. He did not consciously decide not to tell anyone about what he'd found. The decision made itself, the way decisions often did when a boy understood that the thing he'd discovered would sound impossible when put into words.

He would come back. He would watch. He would try to understand what had happened.

He did not know, yet, that this watching would become his life.

---

## Part Two: The Return

He came back four days later, on a morning when his father had sent the smaller herds out with his older brother and his cousin, leaving Luca with an errand that could be stretched into most of the day if he was careful.

The marks were unchanged. The resin on the bark had begun to oxidize, turning a deeper amber. The exposed roots had dried slightly but remained in their new configuration. If anything, the displacement seemed more impossible now that Luca's initial shock had faded. His mind offered explanations more desperately this time: an earthquake, perhaps, too gentle to be widely noticed; a hidden fissure in the limestone that had collapsed; a gradual settling of the ground that had pushed the tree sideways as the earth changed beneath it.

None of these explanations satisfied him.

Over the next month, Luca found reasons to return. His father valued a boy who knew the high pastures, who could find scattered animals quickly and report on conditions. His father valued reliability and a mind for terrain. Luca's father did not scrutinize too closely if his son took slightly longer routes, or stopped to check on something, or climbed a bit higher than necessary to get a better view of the landscape.

But his mother was beginning to notice.

"You're troubled," she said one evening, when Luca had returned from his third visit in a week. "You have that look about you. The one you get when something is bothering the animals."

"Nothing is bothering anything," Luca said, but it was a poor answer.

"You've been ranging farther up the mountain," his father said, with less concern and more observation. "The pastures here in the lowlands are sufficient. There's no need for the herds to go so high, not yet."

Luca had no good answer for this either. In truth, the weather had been stable. The lower pastures were adequate. There was no legitimate reason for him to be climbing toward the high meadow as often as he was. Only the need to return to the tree, to look at the marks again, to try to make sense of what he couldn't explain.

By August, when he returned for perhaps the eighth time, the displacement had grown.

The tree had moved again.

This time, there was no question of interpretation. The new scoring on the stone was directly adjacent to the old marks, extending another two feet in the same direction. The roots had shifted further. The displacement was unmistakable and, to Luca's increasingly certain knowledge, absolutely impossible.

He sat down on a stone and realized he was afraid.

It was not a fear of the tree itself. The tree was still a tree—ancient, passive, rooted in its rock and soil. But the fact of its movement, the clear and undeniable reality of it, was a kind of fear that Luca had never experienced before. It was the fear of discovering that something fundamental about the world was wrong. It was the fear of knowing something that could not be known. It was the fear of being alone with knowledge that had no shape, no name, no place in the world as it was supposed to be.

He forced himself to touch the tree that evening, placing his hand flat against the bark. It was warm from the long afternoon sun. It was solid. It felt like the bark of any other tree he'd ever touched, rough and ancient and utterly ordinary. But underneath that ordinary feeling was the knowledge of what it had done.

He came back three days later and found the marks had changed again. Slightly. Subtly. But changed.

By September, he had lost count of how many times he'd visited. He'd developed a system—a way of comparing the tree's position against particular stones, particular angles of view. He'd noticed that the movement seemed to follow the slope, moving consistently downward and to the west. He'd observed that the movement happened after storms, or during wet periods, or sometimes seemingly at random. He'd found that the tree seemed to prefer moving at night, or at least seemed to have moved overnight more often than during daylight hours.

The village was beginning to gossip.

His mother confronted him directly. "You're in love with a girl," she said, and it was not a question.

"No," Luca said.

"Then what?"

He had no answer that would not sound like madness.

His father was more practical. "There's someone seeing you up there," he said one afternoon. "Jord saw you come down the path last week, moving through the high meadow like you were looking for something specific. If you've found something worth finding, we should know. If you're wasting time, we should address it."

"I'm not wasting time," Luca said.

"Then what?"

There was the question again. What was he doing? There was no practical purpose to his visits. He wasn't searching for lost animals anymore—he'd stopped pretending that was the reason. He wasn't gathering firewood or herbs or anything else with a legitimate use. He was simply watching a tree that moved in ways trees did not move, trying to understand something that understanding seemed to have no framework for.

"I'm thinking," he said finally, and his father seemed to accept this in a way he wouldn't have accepted anything more specific.

But the gossip was spreading. By October, the village had settled on a theory: Luca was meeting someone. A girl from one of the settlements higher up the mountain. A boy from another village. Someone unsuitable, at any rate, which was why he was being so secretive about his absences.

His sister offered to help him meet his alleged lover more discreetly.

His cousin started following him, which forced Luca to be more careful about his route.

By November, he understood that he couldn't continue this way much longer. The visits had to stop, or they had to have a reason that would satisfy the village's curiosity. He couldn't simply disappear into the high meadow three times a week. He couldn't keep returning to the same location without people eventually wondering why, and following him, and discovering what he was doing.

And if people discovered the tree's movement, they would come.

They would cut it down. They would burn it. They would study it and prod it and try to understand it, and in the process of trying to understand it, they would probably kill it.

Luca understood this without anyone telling him. He understood it the way an animal understands when a predator is near.

He was still sitting with this problem, turning it over in his mind like a stone he couldn't quite get into his pocket, when he encountered the monk.

---

## Part Three: The Stranger

The path down from the high meadow was narrow and exposed. Luca had chosen his route carefully—a little-used trail that circled around the visible pastures, coming down through a fold of higher ground where he was less likely to be seen by anyone watching from the village. It was late afternoon, the light already taking on the particular quality of November, that slanting quality that made everything seem to exist in amber.

The man was sitting on a stone beside the path, as if he'd been waiting.

He was older—old enough that Luca couldn't quite determine an age, though his hair was still dark and his build was solid and work-hardened. He wore the rough brown robes of a mountain monk, the kind that the religious orders sent out to tend the isolated shrines and hermitages scattered through the higher elevations. He had no visible weapons, though there was something in his posture that suggested he might not need one.

"Your excuses are becoming worse," the man said, without preamble.

Luca stopped walking.

"Three weeks ago you told your mother you were checking on a sick lamb," the man continued. "Two weeks ago, a broken fence. Last week, a lost goat. Yesterday, a damaged stone shelter that needed repair before winter."

"I don't know you," Luca said.

"No," the man agreed. "But I know you've been to the high meadow at least twice a week for the past two months. I know you're being followed by your cousin, who's beginning to suspect something scandalous. I know your father is running out of patience with vague explanations. And I know," he paused, his dark eyes meeting Luca's, "that you're trying to guard something you don't understand."

"How do you—"

"The tree," the man said. "The old pine on the high slope."

Luca's hand went to a knife he kept at his belt, not to draw it but as a gesture toward the possibility. He was not defenseless, though he was also not entirely sure a knife would matter against someone who moved the way this man seemed to move.

"I'm not here to harm it," the man said. "If I meant harm to the tree, you wouldn't be able to stop me, and I wouldn't have spent three weeks watching you visit it repeatedly while doing nothing at all." He shifted slightly, and Luca realized that the monk's palms, when exposed, showed old scars. Long, white scarring across both palms. Lightning scars, maybe. Or something worse.

"What do you want?" Luca asked.

"To give you advice," the man said. "Your cover story is failing because you're not committing to it. You need something that the village will accept without question. Something that doesn't require repeated explanations or increasingly baroque excuses."

"What?"

"Prayer," the monk said simply. "Tell them you're going up into the high country to pray. Tell them you're troubled by something and you need solitude with God to work through it. Mountain communities accept this. They're skeptical of prayer—most people are—but they also don't question it. It's the one excuse that allows a young person to disappear for hours and ask nothing at all of explanation."

Luca considered this. It was practical advice, the kind of advice that showed the man understood something about how villages worked, how people thought. It was also honest in a strange way. He was troubled. Prayer seemed as reasonable a framing for his troubles as anything else, and it would serve the purpose of letting him continue his visits.

"Who are you?" Luca asked.

"Someone who also knows the tree," the man said. "Someone who's been watching it for longer than you've been alive. Someone who will likely be watching it long after you stop coming to this meadow, one way or another." He stood, moving with an economy of motion that suggested significant strength. "Use the prayer. Tell them you're struggling with faith, or doubt, or whatever it is that young people struggle with. They'll accept it."

"Will you keep watching me?" Luca asked.

"Yes," the man said. "Unless you do something foolish. If you decide to come back with tools to study the tree, or to bring others to see what it's doing, then we'll have a different conversation. But if you're simply protecting it as you're doing now—quietly, without calling attention—then I have no interest in interfering."

He began to walk away, moving down the path with the same unhurried efficiency he'd shown in standing.

"Wait," Luca said. "What happens to it? The tree. What happens to it?"

The man paused without turning around. When he spoke, his voice carried back up the slope in the still afternoon air.

"It moves," he said. "That's what it does. It's been doing it for two hundred years, and it will probably keep doing it for two hundred more. Your job isn't to stop it or explain it. Your job is to make sure the village doesn't find out."

"How am I supposed to do that?"

"By coming back," the man said. "By watching. By learning what it needs. By being here long enough to understand it without anyone else needing to understand it at all." He was walking now, moving steadily down the trail. "Use the prayer. It will work."

And then he was gone, disappeared around a bend of the path with a speed that suggested either urgency or a complete lack of concern with Luca's ability to follow him. Luca stood alone on the narrow trail, the November light turning everything orange and shadow, and understood that something fundamental had changed.

---

## Part Four: The Storm (589 AD)

*Two hundred years earlier.*

The storm came in the late afternoon, the kind of storm that the Pollino mountains produced in their season—a gathering of pressure and moisture that transformed the air itself into something charged and dangerous. The sky had been clear at dawn. By mid-afternoon, the clouds were boiling up from the valleys below, dark and swollen with electricity.

Italus was rooted on the high slope, as it had been rooted for centuries before, deep in limestone soil enriched by the particular combination of minerals that the Pollino exposed. The roots went down perhaps forty feet into the earth, finding crevices and pockets where water could gather, where nutrient-rich soil accumulated. The mycorrhizal network surrounding those roots was older than the tree itself—a vast, patient system of fungal filaments that connected not just to Italus but to dozens of other plants on the slope, creating a slow underground exchange of water and nutrients, communication without words or will.

The bark registered the pressure change.

The needles sensed the shift in air current, the sudden temperature drop, the electric potential building in the layer of atmosphere that the crown reached toward.

This was not a new sensation. Italus had weathered thousands of storms in its centuries of existence. Thunder and lightning were the voice of the sky. The tree bent slightly in the increasing wind, tensioning its wood in ways that distributed the strain, accepting the storm as an ancient animal accepts the seasons—without resistance, simply as the condition of being alive.

The first lightning hit the mountain two miles away, close enough that the sound of it came before the light finished fading. The smell of ozone drifted in on the wind. The second strike hit perhaps a mile distant. The third was close enough that Italus's entire crown registered the static charge in the air as a kind of tingling across ten thousand needle tips.

The man sheltering against the tree—a human being who had come up to the high meadow hours before the storm began, searching for something he could not name—pressed himself closer to the thick trunk as the lightning intensified.

His name was Farovald. He was thirty-nine years old. He had been born in a small settlement two valleys over, had grown up in this mountain country, had spent his adult life wandering the high places where few other people came. He had heard stories, as a child, of something old and strange in the Pollino mountains. Nothing he could quite name or define. Just stories that old people told, fragments of something that had been forgotten.

He had come to the high meadow that afternoon to sit beneath the enormous pine and think about his life, which had accumulated very little of value in thirty-nine years of existence.

When the storm began to move in, he'd been grateful for the shelter. The trunk was so massive that the small area directly against the bark offered some protection from the wind-driven rain.

The lightning was getting closer.

He could feel it in the quality of the air, the way the static made his hair stand up, the taste of ozone on his tongue. The thunder was losing the space that had previously separated it from the light. Thunder and lightning were becoming simultaneous, which meant the strike was coming to this part of the mountain very soon.

He should move, he thought. Should go higher, or lower, or farther away from the tree. Lightning preferred tall things.

But the tree was shelter, and he was afraid, and he stayed.

The next lightning strike hit the crown.

It entered through the highest needle cluster, traveling down through the cambium and heartwood, seeking the path of least resistance downward. Italus's root system, deep in the mineral-rich limestone, conducted the electricity further. The current passed through the fungal network that connected Italus to a dozen other trees and plants, spreading the load. But the tree itself, directly in the path of the strike, received the full initial shock.

The bark nearest the strike blackened. The cambium beneath it cooked. The resin that had accumulated in response to damage from bark beetles and previous storms bled out in hot droplets, boiling at the point where the lightning had passed.

Farovald, pressed against the trunk with his hands flat against the bark, felt the electricity.

It passed through his palms, up his arms, across his chest. It was not enough to kill him—the tree's resistance dissipated much of the charge, and the electrical path through his body lasted only a fraction of a second. But it was enough to mark him. Enough to change something in the deep chemistry of his cells, in the electrical patterns that governed his aging, his healing, the fundamental rate at which his body consumed itself.

When the pain faded, when the smell of scorched resin and burned flesh cleared from the air, Farovald looked at his palms.

They were burned. Deeply burned. The skin was split and blistered, the flesh beneath red and angry. It hurt in a way that was so intense it had temporarily transcended pain and become something else.

The lightning had passed. The storm was moving on.

He stumbled down the mountain in the rain, his hands numb and burning, not understanding that something permanent had just happened to him. He didn't understand, because understanding would require knowledge that didn't yet exist. Understanding would require him to live long enough to realize that the burns on his palms were scarring differently than normal burns did. That the healing was following a trajectory that was possible but unusual. That the scar tissue, when it finally formed, would be dense and white and almost supernaturally perfect.

He didn't understand that he would keep his hands for nearly two thousand years after that afternoon.

That night, Italus's roots were still conducting electricity, the tree's nervous system still firing in patterns that had been disrupted by the strike. The mycelial network was slowly recovering from the shock of having current flow through it. The cambium was damaged but not killed. The resin would flow again, slowly closing the wound. The tree would survive, as it had survived hundreds of other storms.

But something had changed. Something in the structure of the wood, the arrangement of the cells, the subtle mechanics that allowed a tree to remain rooted in one place. The roots seemed to have shifted slightly in the damage. The next day, when the rain cleared and the sun returned, the stone beneath the tree's northeastern base showed marks where something had pressed and moved.

It would take weeks for Italus to understand what had happened. It would take months of night-time movement, small adjustments, testing the limits of what roots and trunk could do, before the full realization would come: it could move. Slowly, expensively, painfully, requiring the expenditure of decades of accumulated energy, but it could move.

It had taken more than five hundred years of static rooting for Italus to understand stillness as its nature. It would take nearly two hundred more before the tree began to understand motion as a possibility, and another century before it began to contemplate motion as a choice.

But the door had opened. The storm in 589 had opened a door that would never close again.

---

## Part Five: The Practice Begins (789, Continued)

Luca returned to the village as the sun was setting.

He told his mother that he had been up on the high slope, in prayer. He told his father the same. He told his sister, when she pressed him for details, that he was troubled about his future, about whether the life of a shepherd was the life he was meant to live, about whether God had other plans for him.

It was not entirely false. He was troubled about these things. And the prayer that happened was real—real in the sense that sitting quietly beside a moving tree, trying to understand its nature, was its own kind of prayer.

Over the following months, as autumn shifted into winter and winter began its slow movement back toward spring, Luca developed a practice.

He would use the prayer as his excuse. He would climb to the high meadow once or twice a week, depending on what could be explained away, and he would spend his time watching and comparing. He kept mental notes of where the tree had moved. He began to understand the pattern—that movement happened more often after heavy rains, that the tree seemed to drift consistently downslope and to the west, that the displacement was small enough that someone not paying close attention might miss it entirely.

He also began to notice other things. The way the resin bled from the damaged bark. The way the roots seemed to organize themselves around the displacement, creating new configurations of strength and anchor. The way the tree's general health seemed not to have suffered from the movement itself—the needles were still thick and vital, the crown was still dense, the bark was still functioning.

By spring, he had developed crude methods to track the displacement. He found a stone some distance from the tree that could serve as a reference point. He created other reference points—a particular combination of rocks, a distinctive growth of low shrub, a stone cairn he built and disguised so that it wouldn't draw attention.

He developed a habit of touching the tree's trunk, placing his palm against the bark. It became a kind of ritual. He would arrive, he would examine the changes, he would place his hand flat against the warm or cool bark, and he would stand that way for a time that might be seconds or might be minutes. What he was hoping to feel, he couldn't have said. Some kind of communication, maybe. Some kind of understanding transmitted through bark and skin. Contact with something that was moving in ways he couldn't explain.

The tree never answered him. But it also never rejected him.

In the early summer of 790, when Luca was nearly fifteen and the village had fully accepted that prayer was indeed his excuse for disappearing into the mountains, the monk appeared again.

This time it was at the village edge, where Luca was herding goats across a lower pasture. The monk simply appeared, moving out of the tree line with the same unhurried efficiency he'd shown before.

"You're doing better," the monk said. "Your cover story is holding. The village accepts your piety."

"Are you going to keep following me?" Luca asked.

"No," the monk said. "I'm going to do something else. I'm going to tell you something, because you're old enough to understand it now, and you're going to need to know it if you're going to keep protecting the tree."

He paused, and Luca realized the monk was genuinely deliberating about how to phrase whatever came next.

"The tree is not supposed to move," the monk said finally. "Trees are supposed to stay rooted. But this tree can move, and it is moving, and it's going to keep moving. The question is whether you want to try to understand what it's doing and help it do it safely, or whether you want to just watch and worry."

"How am I supposed to help it?"

"By learning," the monk said. "By paying attention. By developing enough knowledge of what it needs and what it's capable of that when something goes wrong—and something will go wrong, eventually—you'll know how to respond."

"Something will go wrong?"

"Everything goes wrong eventually," the monk said flatly. "But if you're paying attention, you might be able to make the going-wrong less terrible than it would otherwise be."

Luca considered this. "What's your name?"

"Farovald," the monk said. "That's all you need to know."
